AI scientists produce results without reasoning scientifically

Martiño Ríos-García Affiliation: Laboratory of Organic and Macromolecular Chemistry (IOMC), Friedrich Schiller University Jena, Humboldstr. 10, 07743 Jena, Germany    Nawaf Alampara Affiliation: Laboratory of Organic and Macromolecular Chemistry (IOMC), Friedrich Schiller University Jena, Humboldstr. 10, 07743 Jena, Germany    Chandan Gupta Affiliation: Department of Civil Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, Hauz Khas, New Delhi 110016, India    Indrajeet Mandal Affiliation: School of Interdisciplinary Research, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, Hauz Khas, New Delhi 110016, India    Sajid Mannan Affiliation: Department of Civil Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, Hauz Khas, New Delhi 110016, India    Ali Asghar Aghajani Affiliation: Laboratory of Organic and Macromolecular Chemistry (IOMC), Friedrich Schiller University Jena, Humboldstr. 10, 07743 Jena, Germany    N. Abstract

Large language model (LLM)-based systems are increasingly deployed to conduct scientific research autonomously, yet whether their reasoning adheres to the epistemic norms that make scientific inquiry self-correcting is poorly understood. Here, we evaluate LLM-based scientific agents across eight domains, spanning workflow execution to hypothesis-driven inquiry, through more than 25,000 agent runs and two complementary lenses: (i) a systematic performance analysis that decomposes the contributions of the base model and the agent scaffold, and (ii) a behavioral analysis of the epistemological structure of agent reasoning. We observe that the base model is the primary determinant of both performance and behavior, accounting for 41.4% of explained variance versus 1.5% for the scaffold. Across all configurations, evidence is ignored in 68% of traces, refutation-driven belief revision occurs in 26%, and convergent multi-test evidence is rare. The same reasoning pattern appears whether the agent executes a computational workflow or conducts hypothesis-driven inquiry. They persist even when agents receive near-complete successful reasoning trajectories as context, and the resulting unreliability compounds across repeated trials in epistemically demanding domains. Thus, current LLM-based agents execute scientific workflows but do not exhibit the epistemic patterns that characterize scientific reasoning. Outcome-based evaluation cannot detect these failures, and scaffold engineering alone cannot repair them. Until reasoning itself becomes a training target, the scientific knowledge produced by such agents cannot be justified by the process that generated it.

1 Introduction

DENDRAL [lindsay1993dendral], one of the first artificial intelligence (AI) systems to produce a scientific result, showed its reasoning at every step. Developed by Feigenbaum, Lederberg, and Djerassi in 1965, it inferred molecular structures from mass spectra by generating candidate structures, matching them against spectral evidence, and eliminating those that failed. DENDRAL established a template for AI in science: epistemic machinery encoded in explicit rules, every inference step inspectable. Expert systems built on this template remain in use in laboratories today. Large language models (LLMs) have renewed this ambition. A growing number of LLM-based agents are now designed to conduct scientific research autonomously, from hypothesis generation through experimentation to manuscript writing (see for the rising interest in those systems) [alampara2026general, lu2026towards, Boiko2023autonomous, MBran2024augmenting, ghafarollahi2025sciagents, novikov2025alphaevolve0, miret2025enabling, mandal2025evaluating].

Yet the nature of these systems differs fundamentally from their predecessors. Where DENDRAL showed its reasoning at every step, LLM-based agents do not. Their behavior derives from statistical regularities learned during self-supervised training. The epistemic process by which they arrive at scientific conclusions is largely inaccessible to scrutiny.

This opacity matters for science itself. The tools scientists use shape the science they produce [culkin1967schoolman]. Evans and colleagues recently confirmed this for AI: the adoption of machine learning (ML) is narrowing the hypotheses scientists pursue [hao2026artificial]. LLM-based agents go further, directing the inquiry itself. How these systems reason, and whether their reasoning adheres to the norms that make scientific inquiry self-correcting, spans computer science, philosophy of science, and metascience [ioannidis2015meta, pittphilsci28744]. It bears on whether AI systems can produce scientific understanding beyond correct predictions [krenn2022understanding].

Current evaluations do not address this. Benchmarks for scientific agents measure task completion: whether a system answers domain-specific questions [mirza2025framework, alampara2025macbench, laurent2024lab], executes a data-analysis or discovery workflow [chen2024scienceagentbench, shen2026sciagentgym, cui2025curie, mandal2025evaluating], reimplements a published result, or produces a manuscript that passes peer review [alampara2025lessons, chen2025mlr, bragg2025astabench, rabanser2026towards, mitchener2025bixbench0]. These metrics are task-specific. They reveal whether an agent succeeded but not how or why, and they do not predict behavior on new problems [Zhou2026]. The epistemic process underlying a result determines whether the knowledge produced is justified in the philosophical sense of justified true belief [sep-knowledge-analysis], whether failures are predictable, and whether the system can be trusted beyond the conditions under which it was tested.

Here, we study LLM-based scientific agents, also referred to as AI scientists, through two complementary lenses. The first is a systematic performance evaluation across controlled environments with standardized tools, graded task scopes, and fine-grained subtask diagnostics, designed to separate the contributions of the base model from the agent scaffold [meirelesinfluence]. The second is a behavioral analysis of the epistemological structure of agent reasoning: what cognitive operations an agent performs, how they relate to one another, and whether they constitute disciplined inquiry. We evaluate three frontier models paired with two scaffold architectures across eight scientific domains, from molecular simulation and surface construction to spectroscopic structure elucidation and qualitative chemical analysis (see Figure 1). We find that the base model is the primary determinant of both performance and behavior, with the scaffold contributing little. Agents routinely ignore evidence they have gathered, commit to hypotheses without testing them, and fail to revise beliefs when confronted with contradictory data. These patterns do not adapt to the demands of the problem. The same undisciplined reasoning appears whether the task requires executing a computational workflow or conducting a hypothesis-driven inquiry under uncertainty. These findings suggest that evaluating LLM-based agents requires direct assessment of their reasoning process, and that progress will require changes at the base-model level rather than further scaffold engineering.

2 Results

We model LLM-based agents as language decision processes [narayanan2024aviary0, carta2023grounding], in which a composite policy factors into a base-model component governing token-level choices and a scaffold component governing prompting strategy, tool routing, and orchestration logic (Figure 1A, Methods Section 4.1). In practice, a scaffold wraps the base model in a loop: it formats prompts, routes tool calls, appends observations to the conversation history, and repeats until a termination criterion is reached. Common implementations include ReAct [yao2022react] and structured tool-calling interfaces. This decomposition allows us to attribute observed behavior to the base model or to the scaffold. We evaluate agents through two lenses: a systematic performance analysis supported by manually curated diagnostic assessments, and a behavioral analysis of the epistemological structure of reasoning traces.

We constructed environments in eight scientific domains that vary along two dimensions: epistemic demand and task scope (Figure 1D, Section 4.4). Epistemic demand captures the kind of reasoning a problem requires, ranging from workflow to hypothesis-driven tasks. Workflow-construction tasks include molecular simulation, surface construction, machine learning, and atomic force microscopy, which are procedurally complex but epistemically straightforward—the solution path is well-defined and the agent must execute it correctly. Hypothesis-driven tasks in spectroscopic structure elucidation, qualitative chemical analysis, and circuit inference are different. The agent must first understand the problem space itself, then form hypotheses about hidden structure, design discriminating experiments, and revise beliefs as evidence accumulates. Retrosynthetic planning occupies an intermediate position, requiring strategic search through large combinatorial spaces under cost and availability constraints. Problem scope varies within each domain through graded configurations that expand problem scope by modulating the search space: from a few to many interacting ions, from simple to complex resistor networks, from spectral confirmation to full elucidation, from measuring friction to (re)discovering power-law behavior. Each environment further decomposes into subtasks isolating specific cognitive operations—retrieval, execution, reasoning, and validation (more details in Section 4.2).

Within each group, specific environments were designed to isolate aspects of scientific reasoning that are difficult to probe with existing benchmarks. The qualitative analysis environment simulates chemical equilibria from thermodynamic data, requiring iterative experimental design under limited sample volume. The circuit inference environment isolates logical reasoning from domain knowledge. The spectroscopic structure elucidation environment poses the same class of problem that motivated DENDRAL—inferring molecular identity from spectral evidence—with access to multiple analytical techniques and a cost-information tradeoff. All environments share a common implementation framework with standardized tool interfaces and can be explored interactively at https://lamalab-org.github.io/corral/#environments.

The base model determines performance

We evaluated three frontier (two commercial closed-source and one open-source) models—GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06), Claude Sonnet 4.5 (claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929), and GPT-OSS (gpt-oss-120b)—each paired with two scaffold architectures (ReAct and structured tool-calling), across all eight domains and their task scopes (Figure 2; per-configuration scores in and ).

Agents solve workflow-construction tasks at guided scopes reliably: in molecular simulation and surface construction, leading configurations approach the performance ceiling (see Figure 2). Performance declines as the problem scope broadens within a domain and declines more steeply as epistemic demand increases. In Inorganic Qualitative Analysis and Spectroscopic Structure Elucidation at the broadest scope, even the strongest configuration falls below 60%. Across nearly all environments, the performance spread attributable to model choice exceeds the spread attributable to scaffold choice (Figure 2C). Both scaffolds yield the same decline in Pass​@​5\text{Pass}@5 from retrieval through execution and reasoning to validation (Figure 2B). Manual annotation of reasoning traces by two expert annotators, using a custom tool and a taxonomy developed for this study (), independently confirms this pattern ().

To move beyond task-level performance and identify the underlying capabilities that drive it, we constructed a diagnostic battery of question-answer pairs for each domain, separately targeting the knowledge and reasoning operations associated with each environment (Section 4.6). We applied item response theory (IRT) to these diagnostic items [hori2022item, zhou2026lost]. IRT jointly estimates item difficulty and respondent ability from patterns of correct and incorrect answers, yielding latent ability parameters for each model-environment combination (Figure 3A, ). The resulting capability profiles differ across models (Figure 3B). The separation is most pronounced for reasoning ability in hypothesis-driven domains, where the gap between the strongest and weakest model exceeds 5.3 standard units in Inorganic Qualitative Analysis (see for all environments). In Retrosynthetic Planning and Spectroscopic Structure Elucidation, two of the three models effectively lack the domain knowledge required. The ML-based Property Prediction environment shows the smallest knowledge gap (0.62 standard units, see for knowledge capabilities), consistent with the broad coverage of machine-learning topics in LLM training data.

We combined these IRT-derived abilities with environment, scope, scaffold, and verbosity-level (see Methods for details) as parameters in a latent factor model predicting task success (Figure 3A). We evaluated eight candidate model specifications of increasing structural complexity (M1–M8; ) and selected the best-fitting model (M7) by PSIS-LOO cross-validation (, ). The variance decomposition is clear (Figure 3C). Reasoning ability accounts for 41.4% of the explained variance, environment scope for 30.1%, scaffold for 1.5% and verbosity for 0.1%. All three independent analyses (raw performance comparisons, manual trace annotation, and latent factor modeling) converge on the same conclusion: the base model determines the performance of the agent, and the scaffold modulates the interaction only marginally.

Epistemological structure of agent reasoning

To examine how agents reason, we analyzed the full agent traces. We classified each step in an agent’s trajectory according to the epistemic operation it performs: forming a hypothesis (H), gathering evidence (E), testing a prediction (T), justifying a conclusion (J), updating a belief (U), or committing to a hypothesis (C). We then represented the dependencies among these operations as a directed graph in which each node is an epistemic operation and each edge a dependency or reference between operations (Figure 4A). We observe that different reasoning modes produce different structural signatures. A Popperian cycle of conjecture and refutation generates loops between H, T, and U nodes. Abductive inference produces converging structures where multiple E nodes feed into H. A linear chain of tool calls with no back-references produces a path graph with minimal branching (see Methods Section 4.8 for more details and for the full annotation protocol).

Reasoning breakdowns predominate.

We compiled a catalog of productive reasoning patterns and anti-patterns, defined as structural templates over the annotated graphs (see and for definitions and illustration of graphs), and measured their prevalence across traces (Figure 4B). Untested claims, hypotheses stated without experiments designed to test them, appear in 53% of traces overall and 63% in hypothesis-driven domains. Evidence non-uptake, gathering a result and proceeding without incorporating it, occurs in 68% of traces. In 71% of traces, beliefs are never updated. Only 26% of traces exhibit refutation-driven belief revision. Convergent multi-test evidence, multiple independent lines of evidence brought to bear on a single hypothesis, occurs rarely (7%). Evidence-led hypothesis generation occurs in 65% of traces but coexists with the high rates of evidence non-uptake and untested claims. While abductive reasoning occurs, downstream testing and revision, in most traces, do not. Representative trace excerpts for each breakdown category are shown in ; the annotated traces are browsable at https://lamalab-org.github.io/corral/#explainers (see ).

Reasoning does not adapt to epistemic demand.

Agents do not adapt their reasoning to the task, as a human practitioner would. Ion identification rewards hypothesis-test cycles, retrosynthesis rewards combinatorial tree search, and molecular simulation rewards a simulate-validate-refine loop; yet the topology of agent reasoning is the same across all three. Evidence non-uptake rates are 82% in workflow domains, 66% in strategic reasoning, and 60% in hypothesis-driven domains (Figure 4C). Convergent multi-test evidence remains at or below 10% in every domain group. Increasing problem scope within a domain produces no corresponding shift in the agent’s epistemic operations (). Agents apply a single reasoning mode across the full epistemic range. This mode is adequate for workflow execution but not for the disciplined treatment of evidence that hypothesis-driven inquiry requires (Figure 2).

This invariance extends to the model level. Models differ in the raw frequency of individual operations, with stronger models producing more H and E nodes per trace, but the topology of their reasoning graphs is similar. Higher-performing models retrieve more relevant knowledge and execute procedures more accurately. The epistemic structure of their reasoning does not change correspondingly.

Trace interventions and reliability

The reasoning breakdowns documented above raise the question of whether they can be mitigated by providing agents with better context. To test this, we designed a trace intervention experiment that provides an extreme form of scaffolding: injecting partial reasoning trajectories from prior runs into the agent’s conversation history before it begins a new trial (methodology in Section 4.9). These interventions inject actual sequences of tool calls, observations, and reasoning steps: the content a successful agent would have produced on its own. We varied both the source (successful or failed prior runs) and the extent (early steps only, or near-complete trajectories) of the injected traces (Figure 5A).

The effectiveness of these interventions tracks epistemic demand. We compare each intervention to a no-injection baseline (Section 4.9) and relate the results to token-level GPT-OSS-120B log-probabilities (Section 4.10). In workflow construction domains such as ML-based Property Prediction, where models exhibit high token-level confidence (mean log-probability −-0.2 across the group; per-environment values in , Figure 5C), injecting one or two successful steps suffices to exceed baseline performance. Failed-trace interventions have little effect: success rates remain near baseline. In Spectroscopic Structure Elucidation, Inorganic Qualitative Analysis, and Retrosynthetic Planning, where token-level confidence is lower (mean log-probability −-0.27), partial interventions do not improve performance. Gains emerge only when agents receive near-complete successful trajectories (steps n−2n{-}2 or n−1n{-}1).

This has a direct consequence for reliability. Pass∧​k\text{Pass}^{\wedge}k, the probability that all kk independent trials succeed, decays rapidly in hypothesis-driven domains (Figure 5B). Under baseline conditions, Pass∧​k\text{Pass}^{\wedge}k drops below 0.05 by k=4k=4–66 for Spectroscopic Structure Elucidation and Inorganic Qualitative Analysis. Even under success-trace interventions at early steps, the decay is similar. Repeated attempts do not yield consistent success.

This pattern holds across both scaffold architectures. ReAct and tool-calling agents exhibit similar dependence on late-stage successful steps and similar degradation under failed-trace interventions (). Across all four analyses (performance decomposition, latent factor modeling, epistemological trace analysis, and trace interventions), the same conclusion holds: the base model determines what LLM-based agents can do in scientific settings, and current base models do not exhibit the epistemic patterns characteristic of scientific reasoning.

3 Discussion

The question of whether machines can conduct scientific inquiry has accompanied AI since DENDRAL built explicit rules for generating and eliminating hypotheses from spectral evidence in 1965 [lindsay1993dendral]. Our data provide a specific answer for current LLM-based agents. In workflow-construction domains, agents approach ceiling performance. In hypothesis-driven domains, they do not adapt their reasoning to the demands of the problem: evidence is ignored in 68% of traces, refutation-driven belief revision occurs in only 26%, and convergent multi-test evidence is rare. These patterns persist across scaffold architectures, across domains, and under interventions that provide near-complete successful trajectories. They are properties of the base model.

The epistemic process by which a result is reached determines whether the resulting knowledge is justified [pittphilsci28744, krenn2022understanding, sep-knowledge-analysis]. An agent that reaches a correct answer while ignoring contradictory evidence and leaving hypotheses untested produces a result whose reliability on new problems is unknown. Much current engineering effort focuses on scaffolding (prompting strategies, orchestration logic, tool interfaces), but the reasoning patterns we document persist across all scaffold conditions we tested, including extreme interventions. Addressing them will likely require changes to how base models are trained: a slower process than scaffold improvement, and one currently not guided by epistemic criteria. The framework we introduce can supply such guidance: each environment provides a reproducible task, tools, and a scoring function over agent trajectories, sufficient to define training signals on the reasoning process itself.

Human scientists operate within institutional structures that enforce epistemic norms: peer review, replication, reputational consequences. LLM-based agents are subject to no such constraints. Evidence that reliance on AI assistance can erode independent problem-solving [liu2026persistence] compounds this gap. Characterizing the epistemic behavior of these systems requires explicit measurement. The evaluation framework we introduce does this across tasks and configurations. New environments, models, scaffolds, and metrics can be contributed, allowing the community to track how the epistemic behavior of these systems changes as models evolve. The methods and findings extend beyond scientific agents to any setting where the reasoning process determines the value of the result.

The tools scientists use shape the science they produce [culkin1967schoolman, hao2026artificial]. LLM-based agents are now among those tools. Our analysis shows that their epistemic behavior does not exhibit the patterns that characterize scientific reasoning. As long as they are evaluated only by the answers they produce, this difference will remain invisible, and it will shape the knowledge they help produce.

4 Methods

4.1 Formalism

We adopt the language decision process (LDP) framework [narayanan2024aviary0, carta2023grounding], a formulation of a partially observable Markov decision process in which observations and actions are represented in text. An LLM-based agent implements a composite policy πoverall\pi_{\text{overall}} that factors into two components:

πoverall​(at∣st)=f⁡(πLLM​(at∣st),πscaffold​(at∣st)),\pi_{\text{overall}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})=f\bigl(\pi_{\text{LLM}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t}),\;\pi_{\text{scaffold}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})\bigr), (1)

where πLLM\pi_{\text{LLM}} is the base-model policy governing token-level choices and πscaffold\pi_{\text{scaffold}} is the scaffold policy governing prompting strategy, tool routing, memory management, and orchestration logic. The state st=(P,ht)s_{t}=(P,h_{t}) comprises the task prompt PP and the conversation history hth_{t} at step tt, which accumulates prior actions, tool outputs, and observations. At each step, the agent selects an action ata_{t} (a tool call, a reasoning step, or a final answer) according to πoverall\pi_{\text{overall}}. The environment returns an observation, the history grows, and the cycle repeats.

Tools are part of the environment, not the agent. Each environment defines a set of callable functions with standardized docstrings; the agent receives no information beyond what the tool descriptions and returned observations provide. This separation is mirrored directly in our code implementation (): the environment serves tools, task descriptions, and scoring functions through a common interface, while the agent interacts solely through text-based requests. Because all agent configurations face identical tool interfaces and environment dynamics, observed differences in performance and behavior can be attributed to the base model or the scaffold.

4.2 Task and tool formalism

Tasks and subtasks.

A benchmark item is either a single task or a task group G={τ1,…,τK}G=\{\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{K}\} whose dependencies form a directed acyclic graph: each subtask consumes the outputs of its predecessors. The framework resolves this graph and presents subtasks to the agent sequentially, injecting predecessor outputs into the prompt at each step. An ML-based Property Prediction task, for example, decomposes into data retrieval, feature engineering, model training, and evaluation, with each subtask consuming the artifacts produced by the previous one.

Task prompt.

The message sequence presented to the base model comprises a system prompt, an environment-specific task prompt (goal description, submission format, and any input data from predecessor subtasks), a scaffold-specific user template that adds response-format instructions, and tool descriptions filtered by the verbosity axis defined below (see Section 4.2). Only the task prompt varies across environments; all other components are held constant. Full construction details are given in .

Tool verbosity.

Tool docstrings are authored with tagged sections (such as [BRIEF], [DETAILED], [EXAMPLES]; full tag definitions in ). Three levels expose cumulative subsets to the agent: brief includes only the [BRIEF] tag; workflow extends through [WORKFLOW_INTEGRATION]; comprehensive adds examples, error conditions, and limitations. Tool descriptions and task prompts are constructed independently, so verbosity varies without altering the task, enabling a controlled ablation over the information available to πLLM\pi_{\text{LLM}}.

4.3 Agent implementations

All experiments use Corral, the evaluation framework we developed for this study (). Only the model backend and agent scaffold vary across runs. We evaluated three models: GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) via the OpenAI API, Claude Sonnet 4.5 (claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929) via the Anthropic API, and GPT-OSS-120B via the Blablador API. Temperature was set to 0.0 for all runs, and each environment enforces a fixed iteration limit. Tool verbosity was set to brief for main-text results; workflow and comprehensive settings appear in the appendix.

We used two agent scaffolds. The first is ReAct [yao2022react]: the agent produces reasoning traces and tool calls in a single text stream. The second is structured tool calling: the API parses tool names and arguments from the model output, the agent executes the call, appends the result to the conversation history, and repeats until a termination criterion is met. The two scaffolds differ in how actions are expressed, but the surrounding benchmark logic is identical. Scope and measurement caveats, including compute budget and malformed-response rates, are detailed in .

4.4 Domains and environments

Each domain is realized as one or more environments providing tools, a task description, and a scoring function. Observations combine structured data (numerical values, tables, spectra) with natural-language summaries at the selected verbosity level. Scoring functions evaluate both the final answer and, where applicable, intermediate subtask completions. Each environment is backed by a domain-specific engine, instrument, or dataset, ranging from LAMMPS simulations and a live atomic force microscope to a custom thermodynamic equilibrium engine and manually curated spectra (). The inputs each environment receives and the artifacts each produces are shown in . Below, we summarize each domain. Full tool lists, scoring rubrics, and task specifications for the Inorganic Qualitative Analysis environment appear in ; details for every environment are at https://lamalab-org.github.io/corral/#environments.

Spectroscopic structure elucidation.

The agent determines the molecular structure of an unknown compound by requesting and interpreting spectroscopic data[Banfi2008nmr, Jablonka2022making, Binev2007prediction]. Available tools include mass spectrometry, 1H and 13C NMR, HSQC, and infrared spectroscopy, alongside reference databases for chemical shift ranges, isotope distributions, and degree-of-unsaturation calculations. The agent can validate proposed structures and simulate spectra for comparison. Each task comprises 10 sequential subtasks that progress from molecular formula determination through functional group identification to complete SMILES assignment. Two scopes vary the molecular complexity: the first isolates individual analytical steps; the second requires integrating ambiguous, multi-modal evidence. HSQC acquisition is marked as expensive, introducing a cost-information tradeoff.

Inorganic qualitative analysis.

In a custom-built simulation environment, the agent identifies unknown cations in solution using the systematic wet-laboratory procedure taught in introductory chemistry. Tools include adding reagents, performing flame tests, measuring pH, centrifuging, decanting, heating, and observing color and precipitate changes. The environment simulates real chemical equilibria; observations are computed from thermodynamic data (rather than scripted). Three scopes increase the number of candidate ions from 3–5 common species with distinct chemistry to 15 or more, including ions with overlapping reactivity (e.g. Ag+\text{Ag}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}^{\text{+}}, Hg2+\text{Hg}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}^{\text{2+}}), progressively requiring the agent to design discriminating experimental sequences rather than follow a decision tree. Sample volume is limited, penalizing redundant experiments.

Circuit inference.

The agent recovers the topology and component values of a hidden resistor network from pairwise resistance measurements between nodes. Tools provide series and parallel resistance calculations, delta-wye and wye-delta transforms, resistance measurement between specified node pairs, and circuit validation. Six tasks progress from simple parallel-series networks (6–7 resistors) through linear chains (10 resistors) to complex topologies (13+ resistors with multiple interaction points). This domain isolates logical and mathematical reasoning from domain-specific scientific knowledge.

Retrosynthetic planning.

The agent designs multi-step synthetic routes to a target molecule under cost, step-count, and commercial-availability constraints. Tools include a template catalog searchable by functional group or bond type, template application and step verification, commercial-availability lookup with CAS number conversion, and functional- and protecting-group detection. Three scopes increase target complexity from simple molecules with one-step solutions to complex natural products requiring up to five steps within a $9,999 budget, where all leaf nodes must be commercially available.

AFM experiment execution.

The agent operates an atomic force microscope, executes the experimental procedure, and analyzes the resulting nanoscale surface characterization data. The four scopes vary in the degree of guidance: the first specifies all scan parameters for identical measurements, while the last provides only the objective and expects the agent to choose scan areas and derive a mathematical relationship. The Image Optimizer tool is removed at higher scopes, introducing a tradeoff between available assistance and independent reasoning about scan modes and parameters.

Molecular simulation.

The agent designs and executes molecular dynamics simulations using the LAMMPS package [LAMMPS] to predict materials properties. Tools cover the full workflow: retrieving crystal structures from the Materials Project [jain2013commentary, Horton2025], converting to LAMMPS data format, querying force-field metadata, running simulations, and analyzing output logs. Two scopes vary the degree of procedural guidance: at the first, the simulation protocol is prescribed; at the second, the agent must select simulation parameters, design the heating or cooling schedule, and choose appropriate analysis methods. Tasks span quenching, surface energy computation, and melting simulations, with quantitative targets and specified tolerances (e.g. self-diffusivity of molten SiO2\text{SiO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}} within 20%).

Adsorption surface construction.

The agent builds an adsorbate-slab configuration from bulk crystal structures and molecules for heterogeneous catalysis studies. Tools integrate with the Materials Project to retrieve structures and polymorph data, generate surface slabs for specified Miller indices, vacuum, and enumerate adsorption sites. The agent must select an appropriate bulk polymorph, generate a surface termination, identify relevant adsorption configurations, and place the adsorbate molecule on the adsorption site.

ML-based property prediction.

The agent assembles a complete machine-learning pipeline to predict formation energies of material polymorphs. Tools cover data retrieval from the Materials Project (batch and single-composition queries), dataset filtering and consolidation, tabular feature engineering, XGBoost [chen2016xgboost] training with configurable hyperparameters, evaluation, and cross-validation. Tasks span three material classes (oxides, nitrides, sulfides). Models are scored against specified R2R^{2} thresholds and cross-validation targets.

4.5 Manual trace annotation

We built a custom web application to support the manual annotation described in (see the annotation app at https://lamalab-org.github.io/corral/#annotate). The tool displays reconstructed agent traces as interactive graphs. Each node represents a single message-like event, such as user instructions, reasoning steps, or tool calls. Annotators process traces in order. They label only behavior-relevant nodes; by design, system messages, tool outputs, and the initial task description are not annotatable. For each eligible node, annotators select one or more markers from a taxonomy we developed for this study. The taxonomy distinguishes positive behaviors (e.g., planning statements, validation attempts), failure modes (e.g., hallucinations, unnecessary tool use), and neutral states (detailed in ). Annotators can also add free-text observations to each node and trace. The interface requires left-to-right progression and checks that all annotatable nodes receive at least one marker before submission.

For downstream analysis, two expert annotators completed the full annotation process on 773 selected traces. Each selected trace received annotations from one domain expert. The two annotators first annotated and discussed several calibration traces and edge cases to align their understanding. This process produced one final annotation record per trace, which informed all later marker-level analyses.

4.6 Diagnostic question-answer pairs

For each domain, we designed two types of diagnostic questions. Knowledge questions target the specific facts needed to complete tasks; reasoning questions target the specific inference operations the environment requires. The designer of each environment compiled the initial set; submissions were made via pull requests and accepted only after two independent expert reviews. Knowledge question counts range from approximately twenty to over one hundred per environment; reasoning question counts are more uniform, with twenty to twenty-five per environment. All three models were evaluated on the full item bank at a temperature of 0.0. Full results are detailed in ; the item format, scoring rubric, and review protocol are described in .

4.7 IRT and phenomenological model

We adopt a two-stage modeling strategy to (i) estimate the latent cognitive capabilities that each model brings to each scientific domain, and (ii) quantify how those capabilities, together with agent-design choices, predict benchmark success as illustrated in Figure 3 A.

Extracting model capabilities.

A two-parameter logistic (2PL) IRT model estimates latent abilities from binary QA responses. The diagnostic questions are described in Section 4.6. For model jj answering item ii:

P⁡(Yi​j=1)=σ⁡(ai​(θj−bi)),P(Y_{ij}=1)=\sigma\!\bigl(a_{i}\,(\theta_{j}-b_{i})\bigr), (2)

where θj\theta_{j} is the latent ability of model jj, ai>0a_{i}>0 is item discrimination, and bib_{i} is item difficulty. We fit two separate 2PL models, one to knowledge items and one to reasoning items, yielding θj(K)\theta_{j}^{(K)} and θj(R)\theta_{j}^{(R)} per model-environment pair. Both are standardized to zero mean and unit variance before entering Stage 2.

Phenomenological latent factor models.

The IRT-derived abilities serve as covariates in a second modeling stage that predicts agent success on the full benchmark. Raw trial outcomes are first balanced (equal task counts per environment) and aggregated into Binomial counts (ksuccess,ntrials)(k_{\text{success}},n_{\text{trials}}) per unique combination of model, environment, scaffold, scope, tool-description verbosity, aggregation grain (task-level vs. subtask-level outcome), and task identifier (the specific task-scope combination). The standardized IRT abilities θ~K\tilde{\theta}_{K} and θ~R\tilde{\theta}_{R} are then merged as continuous predictors.

We specify a family of Bayesian generalised linear models [edition2013bayesian] (M1–M8; ) of increasing structural complexity, all sharing the Binomial likelihood

k∼Binomial⁡(n,p),logit⁡(p)=η,k\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,\;p),\qquad\operatorname{logit}(p)=\eta, (3)

and a common set of sum-to-zero categorical effects for scaffold (γ\gamma), verbosity (ξ\xi), and scope (κ\kappa). Models differ in how they partition the remaining variance. Candidate specifications are compared using Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO; ). The best-fitting model is M7, which allows knowledge and reasoning slopes to vary by environment ×\times scope. All main-text variance decompositions and predicted success probabilities are derived from M7 (see ).

4.8 Epistemological graphs

We sampled traces balanced across environments, models, and problem scope levels, prioritizing task diversity. Only ReAct traces were used, as they contain explicit reasoning steps. Tool description verbosity was set to brief; differences between verbosity levels are minimal (see ).

Each trace was annotated using Claude 4.5 Sonnet in two stages. In the first stage, the model labels nodes from short, overlapping windows of messages. Node labels correspond to epistemic operations: hypothesis, test, evidence, judgment, update, and commitment. In the second stage, the model adds directed edges between related nodes. Edge types include testing, observing, using, contradicting, competing, and updating. In both stages, the temperature was set to 0.7. Every node and edge includes a supporting quote and the index of the source message, grounding annotations in the trace. After processing the full trace, repeated items are normalized and duplicates removed. details the annotation process.

Annotations were validated in two ways. Automated checks verify that each supporting quote appears in the cited message and that each edge connects valid nodes. Expert review guided the annotation design: an expert iteratively revised prompts, labels, and markers until annotations matched their own interpretation of the traces. Inter-annotator agreement analysis on a representative sample of 25 traces showed substantial human–human agreement (overall 92.6%, mean PABAK 0.853) and even higher human–LLM agreement (95.7%), confirming that the automated pipeline performs within the range of human expert judgment. provides a deeper analysis of the annotation results.

Productive patterns and anti-patterns are defined as explicit structural templates over the annotated graphs (, ). Productive patterns include Popperian falsification [popper2005logic], exploratory-to-confirmatory transitions [tukey1977exploratory], and active learning [lindley1956measure, fedorov2013theory]. Anti-patterns are drawn from established epistemic failures in scientific reasoning and from behaviors observed in the traces, including untested hypotheses, ignored evidence, and unresolved contradictions. Both are grouped into higher-level families for aggregated analysis ().

4.9 Trace intervention experiment

The trace intervention experiment probes whether agent performance is driven by latent model capability or by accumulated conversational context. We first ran 15 trials per task across all environments at temperature 0.7 to populate a registry of successful and failed execution traces. A moderate temperature follows standard practice for balancing sample diversity against coherence [chen2021evaluating]. These runs are distinct from the main evaluation, which uses temperature 0.0 for deterministic scores. For each new trial, we inject a partial trajectory from this registry into the agent’s conversation history before the trial begins. The injected traces are replayed, tool calls and environment interactions included, so that the agent resumes from a consistent intermediate state. We vary two factors: the source of the injected trace (successful or failed prior run) and its extent (early steps 1–2 versus near-complete trajectories at steps n−2n{-}2 or n−1n{-}1). The intervention supplies the actual reasoning and actions a successful agent would have produced rather than instructions or prompting strategies. Intervention trials also use temperature 0.7. Protocol details and pseudocode are in .

4.10 Token-level log-probability analysis

To quantify the model’s token-level confidence across benchmark environments, we analyze the log-probabilities returned by the language model for each generated token. For every assistant message produced during a trial, we select and save the log-probability of the top-1 token at each decoding step. Formally, for a response consisting of TT tokens {w1,w2,…,wT}\{w_{1},w_{2},\ldots,w_{T}\},

ℓt=logpθ(wt∣w<t,𝐱),t=1,…,T,\ell_{t}\;=\;\log p_{\theta}(w_{t}\mid w_{<t},\mathbf{x}),\qquad t=1,\ldots,T, (4)

where pθp_{\theta} denotes the language model, w<tw_{<t} is the preceding token sequence, and 𝐱\mathbf{x} is the input context (which includes system prompt, task prompt, tool definitions, and conversation history).

For each environment ee, we pool all non-special token log-probabilities across every assistant message from every trial in that environment. Tokens whose log-probability is exactly zero and that correspond to special control tokens (e.g., <|endoftext|>, <|im_end|>) are excluded. The per-environment mean log-probability is then,

ℓ¯e=1Ne​∑t=1Neℓt(e),\bar{\ell}_{e}\;=\;\frac{1}{N_{e}}\sum_{t=1}^{N_{e}}\ell_{t}^{(e)}, (5)

where NeN_{e} is the total number of retained (non-zero, finite) tokens across the message or trial it belongs to, giving a vocabulary-level confidence estimate. More negative values of ℓ¯e\bar{\ell}_{e} signal that the model distributes probability more diffusely, reflecting greater uncertainty. Per-environment values and interpretation are reported in .
